seats: secular academic scholar of the Bible

fixes.row: Forsaken, rejected, forgotten, transgressed, not kept
readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
biblical-theological (literary) teacher
fixes.why: Read in the Berean, all three say the opposite of the label: 'I do not forget Your law' (119:61, 119:109), 'I have not forgotten Your law' (119:153). The row's label word 'forgotten' is matched by the verb, not by what the verse says. A reader scanning the row meets the psalmist's loyalty filed under the people's failure.
fixes.fix: Move Ps 119:61, 119:109 and 119:153 to the row 'Keep, do, walk in, obey the law' (or to 'Loved and delighted in'), where 'not forgetting' is the keeping. Then check the rest of the row for other negated verbs (a verse that denies the label must not stand under it).

fixes.row: Instruction and teaching: a father's, a mother's, a priest's, God's
readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
biblical-theological (literary) teacher
fixes.why: Rule 4 says one sense of a word is never presented as its whole, and the note says honestly that the Hebrew is one word. But the split is made by MACULA's gloss, not by the text, and it cuts apart what belongs together. Isa 5:24 ('they have rejected the instruction of the LORD of Hosts') is the same rejection of the LORD's torah as Amos 2:4, yet it is absent from 'Forsaken, rejected'. Isa 30:9 ('unwilling to obey the LORD's instruction') is absent from 'Keep, do, obey'. Hos 8:12 (Berean: 'the great things of My law', written by God) and Isa 8:20 (Berean: 'To the law and to the testimony!') are printed 'law' by the Berean and read as the written law, yet the law rows do not show them. The same gloss test is applied inconsistently: Isa 2:3 is kept in the law sense because it parallels Mic 4:2, while verses the Berean prints 'law' (Isa 8:16, 8:20, Jer 18:18, Hos 8:12, Mal 2:9) are moved out. The result is that the law rows undercount the prophets' charge of rejecting the LORD's torah and the priests' duty to teach it, and the instruction row looks like a separate genre of wisdom sayings when God's and the priest's torah is the same thing the law rows describe.
fixes.fix: Keep the row, but follow the hub's own rule that a verse sits in every row it fits: also list Isa 5:24, Hos 8:12, Isa 1:10 (the LORD's instruction heard) and Mal 2:9 in 'Forsaken, rejected'; Isa 30:9 and Exod 16:4 in 'Keep, do, walk in, obey' (walk in My instruction / unwilling to obey); Isa 8:20 in 'Beside the covenant ... testimony'; Mal 2:6-9 and Jer 18:18 in 'Taught and read aloud; the priests'. Add one sentence to the note: 'The line between instruction and law here is MACULA's gloss; where the Berean prints law the same verse also stands in the law rows.' Re-test Isa 2:3 against the same rule so the hub does not apply a parallel-verse test to one verse and a gloss test to the rest.

fixes.row: Instruction and teaching: a father's, a mother's, a priest's, God's
readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
fixes.why: The Berean reads 'Is this Your custom with man, O Lord GOD?'. The verse says nothing of instruction or teaching, and the Hebrew torat ha'adam is among the hardest phrases in Samuel. Filing it under 'a father's, a mother's, a priest's, God's' teaching shows a reader a verse that does not show its label, and settles a disputed phrase by the row it is put in.
fixes.fix: Move 2 Sam 7:19 to 'Every other use' with a short note that the Hebrew word is torah and the Berean prints 'custom', or keep it here with a note in the row saying the phrase is uncertain and the Berean's word is 'custom'.

readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
biblical-theological (literary) teacher
fixes.why: Rule 6: the first example shown is Rom 3:27, whose Berean text ('On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith.') has the word faith but not law. The reader sees the example under 'The law, and faith' and cannot find the law in it; only the note explains why. Counted: 24 of 25 rows show their label in all four examples, this is the one that does not.
fixes.fix: Take Rom 3:27 out of the four shown examples and put Rom 3:28, Rom 4:14, Gal 3:12 or Phil 3:9 in its place (all show both 'law' and 'faith' in the Berean). Keep Rom 3:27 inside the row with its existing note.

fixes.row: Died to the law, released from it, not under it, redeemed from its curse; “Christ is the end of the law”; “abolished in His flesh”; “a change of law”
readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
biblical-theological (literary) teacher
fixes.why: Three problems of weight in the contested block. (1) Rom 10:4: the note says τέλος means end, goal or completion and the page does not choose, but the verse is placed only in the 'ended' row and its label quotes the Berean's 'end'. A row that quotes one of the three renderings in its label does choose. The goal/completion reading is the one that fits rows 21 and 23 and it is not shown there. (2) 'Not under it' (Rom 6:14-15, Gal 5:18) is the phrase whose meaning is exactly what is disputed (condemnation, covenant sphere, power of sin); putting it in a row with 'died', 'released', 'abolished' and 'change' makes it read as the law ending. (3) Heb 7:19 ('the law made nothing perfect') says what Heb 10:1 says ('can never make perfect'), but Heb 10:1 sits in the 'before / guardian / shadow' row and Heb 7:19 in the 'ended' row, so the same claim is filed on two sides. The row is also the longest label of the three (six phrases against four and four), which makes 'ended' the heaviest visually.
fixes.fix: (1) Drop 'Christ is the end of the law' from the label and give τέλος a short neutral place in the note ('Rom 10:4, the Berean's “end”: the Greek τέλος is end, goal or completion'); also list Rom 10:4 in row 21 (Gal 3:24, 'to lead us to Christ') or row 23 so the goal reading is as visible as the end reading. (2) Move Rom 6:14, 6:15 and Gal 5:18 out of this row (they remain in 'Under the law' and 'The law, and grace'), or relabel the row so 'not under it' is not presented as a release. (3) Move Heb 7:19 beside Heb 10:1 in row 21. (4) Shorten the label to the same length as the other two, for example: “Died to the law”; “released from the law”; “abolished in His flesh”; “a change of law”.

fixes.row: “Not to abolish but to fulfill”; “we uphold the law”; not the least stroke will pass; summed up and fulfilled in love
readers: biblical-theological (literary) teacher
fixes.why: The row's own word is 'fulfill', and it holds 'a verse sits in every row it fits'. Gal 6:2 ('you will fulfill the law of Christ') and Luke 24:44 ('Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses') use the same verb and are not in the row, so the fulfill language is split from the 'fulfill' row. Without them the row is the thinner of the contested set in the story's own terms (fulfilment as the Gospel arc), and the page can look as though continuing is argued less than ended.
fixes.fix: Add Gal 6:2 and Luke 24:44 to this row (both already stand in other rows). Leave out Luke 16:16 unless a reason is given; it is about the law and the prophets 'until John' and fits the row 'Before the law was given' better, as a statement of time.

fixes.row: Three contested rows and the row after them
readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
biblical-theological (literary) teacher
fixes.why: The three contested rows are placed 21, 22, 23 alphabetically, but the next and last real row is 'Jesus speaks of the law', whose lead verses are Matt 5:17 and Luke 24:44, which are the 'fulfil' verses. That makes the order read: law added / ended / fulfilled, then Jesus on fulfilling. The last thing a reader meets is the 'fulfill' side. Equally, putting Jesus' own words before the block would make them look like the premise of Paul's. Either position is a tilt; the row says in its note that it takes no side, but its position does. Also 'Jesus speaks' has 15 verses, 12 of them already in other rows (a row that repeats rather than adds, rule 7).
fixes.fix: Move 'Jesus speaks of the law' to sit with the Gospels' sayings before the contested block (after 'The Law and the Prophets' is the natural place), so the block 21-23 is the last section and closes without a Jesus row after it. Alternatively merge it into the 'The Law and the Prophets' row's neighbours and drop the separate row to bring the count to 24.

fixes.row: Beside the covenant and the promise; the testimony, statutes, ordinances (also “justice”) and commandments
readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
biblical-theological (literary) teacher
fixes.why: The label opens with 'the covenant and the promise', but of the 69 verses only about a dozen name a covenant or the promise (Gal 3, Rom 4, Hos 8:1, Ps 78:10, Jer 31:33, Heb 8:10, Isa 24:5, 2 Kgs 17:34). The rest name the law beside its statutes, commandments, ordinances and testimonies (Gen 26:5, Exod 24:12, the Neh 9 verses, Ps 19:7). The label therefore reads the row as 'law and promise' (the Pauline frame of Gal 3) when most of the Old Testament verses are about the law beside its own synonyms. 'Promise' (ἐπαγγελία) is a New Testament term put first in a row whose Old Testament verses hold covenant and statute, a rule 5 problem of order. Verses where the beside-word is 'justice' (Hab 1:4, Isa 42:4, Isa 51:4) and 'righteous standard' (Rom 8:4) are stretched to 'ordinances' by the label. A 69-verse row with two sorts is also hard to read.
fixes.fix: Split in two. 'Beside the covenant; the promise' (about 15 to 20 verses: Gal 3:17, 3:18, 3:21; Rom 4:13-16; Jer 31:33; Heb 8:10, 10:16; Hos 8:1; Ps 78:10; Isa 24:5; Deut 29:21; 2 Kgs 17:34-37). And 'Beside its statutes, commandments, ordinances and testimonies (also “justice”)' for the rest. Put the covenant half first, with the Old Testament covenant verses ahead of Gal 3 and Rom 4. In the second label, add 'righteous standard' for Rom 8:4 or remove it from the row.

fixes.row: Taught and read aloud; the priests, Levites, scribes and Pharisees
readers: biblical-theological (literary) teacher
fixes.why: At 59 verses this row holds two things under one label: the law being read and taught (Deut 31, Neh 8, Ezra 7:10, Acts 13:15) and the law beside a class of people (priests offering by the law, Heb 7:28 and 8:4, Lev 7:7 and 14:2, Phil 3:5 'as to the law, a Pharisee', Matt 12:5). Heb 7:28 and 8:4 neither teach nor read; they say the law appoints high priests, which belongs with Heb 7:12 ('when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed') in the story of priesthood and law, and that pair is cut apart (7:12 is in the contested block, 7:28 here). Lines about Pharisees and scribes in the label are New Testament groups heading a row that mainly holds the Old Testament's reading and teaching.
fixes.fix: Split into 'Read aloud and taught' (Deut 31, Neh 8, Ezra 7:10, 2 Chr 17:9, Acts 13:15, Ps 94:12, Isa 2:3, Mic 4:2) and 'The priests, Levites, scribes and Pharisees beside the law' (the others). Add a one-line note on the second pointing at Heb 7:12 and 7:28, and 8:4 together, so the priesthood-and-law verses are visible as one set.

readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
fixes.why: 'The Law and the Prophets' is the New Testament's name for the Scriptures as two divisions (Matt 5:17, Luke 16:16, Acts 24:14). The seven Old Testament verses do not use the phrase and do not name two divisions; they name the law and prophets as two things God sent or two things a people refused (Zeph 3:4, Lam 2:9, Jer 2:8). Filed under that heading with no note, they read as if the Old Testament already spoke of a canon in two parts, which is a later development read back into earlier texts.
fixes.fix: Add a note: 'In the New Testament “the Law and the Prophets” names the Scriptures. The Old Testament verses here name the law and the prophets side by side as what God sent and the people refused; they do not use the phrase as a name.' Or relabel: 'The law beside the prophets; “the Law and the Prophets”'.

readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
biblical-theological (literary) teacher
fixes.why: About ten Old Testament verses stand both here and in 'Forsaken, rejected, forgotten, transgressed' (Amos 2:4, Dan 9:11, Neh 9:29, Jer 44:23, Rom 2:23, Jas 2:9 and others): the same verses under two labels that say nearly the same, which is the rule 7 'rows that say the same thing'. In the Old Testament the people's sin is forsaking the law, so a reader meets the same set twice. What the row adds is the New Testament's saying that the law brings knowledge of sin and the Deuteronomic curse, and the label does not separate the two.
fixes.fix: Leave the Old Testament transgression verses in 'Forsaken ...' only, and make this row 'The law and sin; the curse', holding Rom 3:20, 4:15, 5:13, 5:20, 7:5-14, 1 Cor 15:56, 1 Tim 1:9, Gal 3:10, 3:13, 3:19 and Deut 27:26, 29:21, Josh 8:34 (the curse written in the book of the law). That takes about eight verses out and leaves the two rows reading differently.

fixes.row: The law, and faith, believing / The law, and works
readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
fixes.why: Five of the nine verses of 'The law, and works' (Rom 3:27, 3:28, Gal 2:16, 3:2, 3:5) are also in the faith row; the note says so. Two rows that share more than half of the smaller are in practice one passage set (Paul's 'works of the law' against 'faith') shown twice. A reader may take the two rows as a faith-versus-works frame, which is Paul's argument but not the form of the law's other verses.
fixes.fix: Optional: merge into one row 'The law, faith and works' (about 23 verses) with the existing no-side note; or keep both and add to the works row a line saying its verses are drawn from the faith row where both words stand. Lower priority than the fixes above.

readers: secular academic scholar of the Bible
fixes.why: The Berean prints 'those who are under the law' in Rom 3:19, so a reader searching the row for the phrase will not find it and may think the page missed it. The Greek is ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ('in the law'), so excluding it is right by the original, but the row does not say.
fixes.fix: Add to the note: 'Rom 3:19 reads “under the law” in the Berean; the Greek is “in the law” (ἐν) and the verse is under Every other use.' Keep it out of the row.

worker_points.point: 1(a). Order and weight of the three contested rows (A, D, N)
worker_points.why: The alphabetical order is neutral, but the middle row has the longest label, carries 'not under it' and Rom 10:4's 'end' as its own phrases, and the row after the block (Jesus speaks) ends on the fulfil side. See the tilt fixes: shorten the label to match, move Jesus' row ahead of the block, move Heb 7:19 beside Heb 10:1.

The note is honest, but the label quotes 'end' and the verse is only in the 'ended' row. Take the quote out of the label and show it also in the guardian/goal row or the fulfil row, so that all three of end, goal and completion are visible.

'Guardian to lead us to Christ' says 'until', 'to lead' and 'that we might be justified by faith', which is time and purpose, so it fits row 21. Gal 3:25 has no νόμος, so leaving it out is right. One addition: put Rom 10:4 beside it (the 'goal' reading).
None of the three labels or notes names a scheme. 'Guardian', 'shadow' and 'added because of transgressions' are the text's own words.

worker_points.point: 2. Faith, works, grace rows and Rom 3:27 shown with 'principle'
worker_points.why: Showing the Berean's 'principle' is correct by the original. But Rom 3:27 as a lead example under 'The law, and faith' shows no law; replace the example (see the label fix). The grace row is fine: John 1:17 and Rom 6:14 are quoted as written and the note names three ways traditions read.

worker_points.point: 3. 'Under the law' (8 verses, ὑπό next to νόμος)
worker_points.why: The ὑπό rule is right and Rom 3:19 is correctly out (ἐν). Add a note on Rom 3:19 since the Berean prints 'under the law' there. The 1 Cor 9:20 parenthesis is quoted fairly.

worker_points.point: 4(a). Row 11: one Hebrew word, instruction and law
worker_points.why: Saying it is one word is correct and good. The inconsistency is that the verses are sorted by MACULA's gloss rather than the text, so Isa 5:24, Isa 30:9, Hos 8:12 and others are missing from the law rows where they belong; and 2 Sam 7:19 does not show its label. See the fixes.

Every example shows 'This is the law ...' in the Berean; the Berean's 'skin diseases and mildew' is used. The note's reference to 'the three rows at the end' makes the Torah's rulings sound like the subject of the contested rows; that is not what those rows say (Heb 10:1 and Heb 7 name the priesthood and sacrifices, the others name 'the law' generally). Soften: 'the three rows at the end set out what the New Testament says of the law as a whole.'

worker_points.point: 4(c). Row 10: law for the foreigner beside Isa 2:3 and Rom 2:14
worker_points.why: The Old Testament verses (Exod 12:49, Num 15:29, Isa 2:3) lead and Rom 2:14 follows. Phil 3:5 and John 7:23 are about circumcision only, not foreigners, and the label does say circumcision; they sit a little oddly, but they do not mislead.

Jer 31:33 leads, the Hebrews quotations name it, and Rom 2:15 and Rom 7:23, 7:25 speak of the heart and mind. The note says nothing of how they relate beyond saying the traditions part. For a scholar the Rom 7:23, 7:25 'law of my mind' is a looser fit with 'written on the heart' than the others; the label 'in the mind' covers it.

Keeping 1 Cor 9:21 under the other words is right (different Greek word). Rom 9:31 'a law of righteousness' is in the row but not named in the label; add it to the label list or note so the list is complete.
'The law of the LORD, of God' comes from adjacency to the divine names, and Jesus and Christ are by hand (Gal 6:2, Rom 8:2 and the Jesus row). Nothing infers a person from a rule.

worker_points.point: 7. Heb 9:19, Acts 7:53, Gal 3:19 in 'Given through Moses'
worker_points.why: The note says these name angels and a mediator, not Moses, and the label ('given') fits them. Gal 3:19's 'mediator' is not said to be Moses and the page does not say it is.

missing.what: The law's own account of its place in the story: Gen 26:5 (Abraham 'kept My laws') is in the keeping row only and is not set against Rom 5:13 'before the law was given'; the arc of the book found and read (2 Kgs 22:8-11, Neh 8) is spread over two rows. The 'law in time' row (21) holds only New Testament verses, so the Old Testament's own sequence (given at Sinai, set beside the ark, found, read, promised on the heart, going out from Zion) is not shown as a sequence. A short note on row 21, or its Old Testament counterpart, would let the story's arc show without a side taken.

Ps 119:44 and the Psalter's 'forever' for the law (the law kept 'forever and ever'), and Mal 4:4 'Remember the law of Moses', are in the keep row and the Moses row but not shown as a thread for the law's continuing, while the New Testament side has 'end' and 'abolished'. This is not a call to add a verdict; it is that a reader looking for what the Old Testament says of the law's duration finds it only by scanning.

examples_checked: 24 of 25 rows' examples show their label (all four examples read in the Berean for every row; Rom 3:27 under 'The law, and faith, believing' shows faith but not the word law). Also read in the Berean and found to contradict their row: Ps 119:61, 119:109, 119:153 ('do not forget Your law') under 'Forsaken ... forgotten'.
summary: The Torah rows are sound and honest about the one Hebrew word, and the no-side notes keep to the text, but a few verses contradict their row (Ps 119:61, 109, 153), the instruction/law split is made by a gloss and leaves Isa 5:24, Isa 30:9 and Hos 8:12 out of the law rows where they belong, and the middle contested row and the Jesus row after it tilt the block. Fix those, split the two overlong rows (covenant-and-statutes; teaching-and-priests) and move Rom 3:27 out of the shown examples, and the hub can ship.
